title: A Brief Overview of Punk Rock
summary: Josh and Chuck give an overview of punk rock, framing it as a culture and movement rather than just a sound. They discuss proto-punk precursors (New York Dolls, Los Saicos, Stooges, MC5, Death), the New York scene around CBGB and the Ramones, the London scene and the Sex Pistols' 1976 Manchester show, the DIY ethos (Buzzcocks' Spiral Scratch, independent labels, zines, distribution via the Cartel), the major-label signing frenzy and what happened to indie labels, Sid Vicious's death and the shift to hardcore in LA and DC, UK versus US politics, punk fashion, pop punk and the commodification debate, and the legacy of punk. The episode ends with listener mail about colostomies and a sign-off.

entities.name: Once Upon a Time in Hollywood

segments.title: Opening banter and punk as culture
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode, acknowledge punk fans may object to a single-episode overview, and discuss punk as a culture and movement with many subgenres. They talk about their own favorite bands and the New York Dolls as a proto-punk predecessor.

segments.title: Punk as reaction to bloated rock
segments.summary: Punk is framed as a reaction against long songs, arena rock and commercialized rock in the 1970s. The Ramones' origins are described, and the 1977 album landscape is contrasted with punk's rebellion.

segments.title: Proto-punk precursors and punk guitar style
segments.summary: The hosts discuss early proto-punk bands, including Los Saicos from Peru, the Chocolate Watchband, and the Stooges, MC5 and Death from Michigan and Detroit. They also describe the downstroke guitar style associated with punk.

segments.title: New York scene at CBGB
segments.summary: CBGB, run by Hilly Kristal, becomes the center of the New York scene, with the Ramones, Talking Heads, Blondie and Television playing there. Max's Kansas City and the Velvet Underground connection are mentioned, along with heroin use in the scene.

segments.title: London, Manchester and the Sex Pistols
segments.summary: The hosts compare the New York and London scenes, mention Australia and other parallel scenes, and describe the Ramones' 1976 London shows and the Damned's 1977 US tour. They describe the Sex Pistols' June 1976 Manchester show as a starting point for UK punk.

segments.title: DIY origins and independent labels
segments.summary: Punk's do-it-yourself ethos is discussed, including cheap recording gear, self-started labels like Step Forward, Fast Product and Factory Records, and the Damned's 'New Rose' as an early single. Buzzcocks' Spiral Scratch EP is described along with its instructions printed on the sleeve. Distribution through the Cartel and zines are covered.

segments.title: Major label signings and the fate of indie labels
segments.summary: Major labels quickly signed UK punk acts within months of the Sex Pistols' first show, including the Clash, the Jam, Generation X and the Buzzcocks' label move. Independent labels either were absorbed, grew into larger indie labels such as Rough Trade and Factory, or stayed underground. The hosts discuss the death of Sid Vicious in February 1979 and the transition to hardcore.

segments.title: Hardcore, LA and DC scenes and UK versus US punk
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Los Angeles punk scene, Penelope Spheeris's film The Decline of Western Civilization, and Washington DC's Bad Brains. They compare US hardcore's masculine, serious tone with UK punk's political and glam-influenced, less serious approach. Post-punk bands such as Hüsker Dü, the Minutemen and Sonic Youth, and the line toward Nirvana, are mentioned.

segments.title: Punk fashion, pop punk and punk as commodity
segments.summary: Punk fashion is discussed, including safety pins, ripped jeans, Richard Hell, the New York Dolls and thrift-store clothing in LA. Malcolm McLaren's role in shaping the Sex Pistols and promoting his shop's clothing is noted. Pop punk bands such as Green Day, Blink-182 and Rancid are discussed, along with Fugazi as a DIY band that stayed independent.
